h1: Beer with Indian sweets beyond the festive season
title: Beer With Indian Sweets All Year Round | Craft Beer School
desc: How to pair gulab jamun, rasgulla, jalebi, kheer and other Indian sweets with beer, using sweetness, spice and texture.
teaser: Gulab jamun with a dry lager tastes like sugar and tin. Pick the right beer and it tastes like a proper dessert course.
standfirst: Indian sweets are some of the sweetest desserts in the world, which makes them a real test for beer. Festive pairings get all the attention, but mithai is eaten all year. Here is how to match it with sweetness, spice and texture in mind.
sections:
The one rule that never bends in dessert pairing is this: the drink must be at least as sweet as the dessert. When it is not, the dessert strips the drink of its own sweetness and leaves only bitterness and acid. A light lager with a gulab jamun tastes thin and slightly metallic for exactly this reason.

Indian sweets are very sweet. A gulab jamun soaked in syrup or a piece of jalebi sits far above most beers in sugar. So we start with the fuller, sweeter end of beer: milk stouts, imperial stouts, Belgian dubbels and quadrupels, Scotch ales, barley wines and fruit beers. These finish with more residual sugar, often 1.020 or above on the hydrometer, against around 1.008 to 1.012 for most lagers.
Syrup-soaked sweets want dark, rich beer

Gulab jamun, jalebi, imarti and malpua are fried, then soaked in sugar syrup, often scented with cardamom, rose or saffron.

  • Gulab jamun: an imperial stout or a Baltic porter. The roast and dark chocolate flavours stand up to the fried khoya and syrup.
  • Jalebi: a Belgian dubbel or a barley wine. Their caramel and dried fruit notes meet the crisp caramelised batter.
  • Malpua with rabri: a milk stout, whose creaminess echoes the rabri.

These beers are strong, usually 7 to 12% ABV. Serve 100 to 150 ml, as you would a dessert wine.
Milk sweets want creamy, gentle beers

Rasgulla, rasmalai, sandesh, kalakand and kheer are built on milk. They are sweet but gentler, with cardamom, saffron and pistachio.

A milk stout or an oatmeal stout matches their creaminess. A hefeweizen, with banana and clove from the yeast, is a lovely partner for rasmalai, because clove and cardamom are close relatives on the palate. A Belgian witbier works with kheer or payasam made with jaggery, where coriander and orange peel lift the rice and milk.

Avoid heavily roasted, bitter stouts with delicate sandesh. The roast will flatten the subtle milk flavour.

Mysore pak, besan ladoo, sohan halwa, kaju katli and gajar halwa are rich with ghee, nuts or gram flour. Nutty and toasty sweets love nutty, toasty beers.

  • Mysore pak or besan ladoo: an English brown ale or a Scotch ale, with toffee and nut flavours from crystal malt.
  • Kaju katli: a brown ale or a mild, gentle enough for a delicate sweet.
  • Gajar halwa: a Belgian dubbel, whose dark fruit and spice suit the carrot, ghee and cardamom.

Ghee is fat, so a little carbonation helps here. Bottle-conditioned Belgian ales tend to be lively, which keeps a rich halwa from feeling heavy.

Cardamom, saffron, rose, nutmeg and clove do the matchmaking. Look for the same notes in the beer:

  • Clove and banana in a hefeweizen meet cardamom and nutmeg.
  • Dried fruit and spice in a dubbel meet saffron and dry fruits in a sweet.
  • Coffee and chocolate in a stout meet fried, caramelised sweets.
  • Real fruit in a kriek or raspberry beer meets rose and fruit-based sweets.

Our guides to Indian food and beer pairing and Diwali beer pairing carry the same thinking into a full meal.

Festivals bring mixed boxes, but most of us buy mithai year-round: a box of jalebi with Sunday breakfast, a sweet shop visit after dinner, modaks around Ganesh Chaturthi, sandesh in Kolkata any month of the year. Treat a single sweet as a small dessert course with one small beer, not as a sweet platter with a drinking session.

Many sweets are eaten in family settings with guests who do not drink. Keep good non-alcoholic choices on the table: masala chai, filter coffee or a non-alcoholic wheat beer all pair well with mithai.
Try one sweet with two beers

Pairing claims are easy to make and easy to test. Buy two gulab jamuns and two very different beers, a dry lager and a milk stout. Taste the sweet, then the lager. Then a fresh bite and the stout.

You will notice the lager turn thin and bitter while the stout holds its body. That difference is the sweetness rule in action. Once you have tasted it you will see it everywhere. Your first step is that test this week. Write down what happened to the beer's bitterness each time. That one note will guide every dessert pairing you make.
faqs: What beer goes with gulab jamun?
A rich, sweet beer such as an imperial stout or Baltic porter. A light lager tastes thin and bitter next to the syrup.
Why does beer taste bitter with sweets?
Sugar in the dessert masks the beer's own sweetness, leaving bitterness and acid. Pick a beer at least as sweet as the dessert.
What beer suits rasmalai or kheer?
A milk stout, oatmeal stout or hefeweizen. Their creaminess and gentle spice suit milk-based sweets.
How much beer should I serve with dessert?
About 100 to 150 ml of a strong dessert beer, as you would a dessert wine. Offer chai, coffee or a non-alcoholic option too.
